stem: Why is a misleading-success tool result considered more dangerous than an explicit error?

options.text: Because nothing on the surface signals a problem, so the agent may accept a wrong or incomplete result without any prompt to double-check it
Because explicit errors are always impossible to recover from
Because misleading-success results always crash the entire system
There is no meaningful difference in danger between the two

explanation.why_correct: An explicit error at least signals that something went wrong, prompting a response; a misleading-success result gives no such signal, so a wrong or incomplete result can be accepted and acted upon without any trigger to double-check it.

why_incorrect.B: Explicit errors are often quite recoverable (e.g. correcting input and retrying); they are not inherently unrecoverable.
why_incorrect.C: Misleading-success results don't crash anything; the danger is specifically that execution continues normally on faulty information.
why_incorrect.D: There is a meaningful and important difference: one has a visible signal prompting a response, the other does not.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Misleading-success results are more dangerous precisely because they provide no error signal to prompt scrutiny, unlike explicit errors.

stem: Match each retry-design element on the left to the specific risk it controls on the right. One risk on the right is not controlled by any listed element.

left.text: Backoff delay that grows between attempts
A unique idempotency key attached to a write call
Classifying a failure as transient or persistent before retrying

right.text: Applying a side effect twice when a timed-out action had actually succeeded
Retrying a cause that waiting cannot fix, such as a permanently invalid credential
Piling extra load onto a service that is already struggling
Spending unbounded time and resources on a call that may never succeed
Accepting an empty result set as proof that nothing exists

explanation.why_correct: Backoff spaces out attempts so a struggling service is not flooded. A maximum attempt count bounds the time and resources spent on a call that may never succeed. An idempotency key lets a retried write be recognized as the same request, so a timed-out action that actually succeeded is not applied twice. Classifying the failure as transient or persistent before retrying avoids retrying causes that waiting cannot fix, such as an invalid credential. Accepting an empty result as a true negative is a sanity-checking concern, not a retry-design one.
explanation.rule_of_thumb: Backoff protects the service, the cap protects your budget, idempotency protects against duplicates, and classification avoids pointless retries.

stem: A team designs an agent with only one single tool for retrieving pricing data, with no alternative source of any kind if that tool is ever unavailable. What risk does this design create?

options.text: An automatic doubling of the tool's reliability
No risk at all, since a single tool is always more reliable than multiple
Guaranteed success on every single pricing request forever
A single point of failure, where the pricing task simply cannot proceed if that one tool fails or becomes unavailable

explanation.why_correct: With no fallback and only one tool for pricing data, any failure or unavailability of that single tool leaves the agent with no alternative path, making it a single point of failure for the entire pricing task.

why_incorrect.B: Having only one source does not inherently improve reliability; it removes the resilience that an alternative fallback path would provide.
why_incorrect.C: A single tool with no fallback does not guarantee success; it is, if anything, more exposed to failure with no alternative to fall back on.
why_incorrect.A: Using only one tool has no mechanism by which its reliability would double; this is not how redundancy or reliability works.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Relying on a single tool with no fallback creates a single point of failure for whatever task depends on it.
